paper_title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are hot topic (Ansari et al., 2024; Das et al., 2023; Ansari et al., 2025; Jain & Sen, 2026; Cohen et al., 2025). The field is growing fast: Every year, new models are released that refresh the leaderboard. The models are commonly evaluated through point accuracy (e.g., MASE) and marginal probabilistic scores (e.g., CRPS, scaled quantile loss) (Aksu et al., 2024; Shchur et al., 2025). Consequently, most of the recent TSFMs are designed and trained to produce quantile levels, which are optimized for these benchmarks. Point accuracy and marginal probabilistic scores are widely adopted for good reason: they provide an interpretable, per-step summary of forecast quality that directly supports common operational decisions such as inventory planning, resource allocation, and risk management. However, they do not capture all aspects of forecast quality. Other properties, particularly trajectory-dependent ones, are important but overlooked by these metrics. Among many, we illustrate two important aspects: Learning distributions with multiple modes: Quantiles are defined through the inverse of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the target distribution. These CDFs, however, are not always nice and smooth, for instance, when the target distribution has multiple modes or sharp peaks. With few or few dozens of quantiles, the resulting approximation of the CDF can be quite rough and suffer from regression-to-the-mean issue (Yu et al., 2026). See the Lorenz oscillator example in Figure 1. Learning autocorrelation: Many quantile regression models predict marginal quantiles at individual time steps across forecast window. Ad hoc methods have been proposed to mitigate these weaknesses, such as completing marginal quantiles under independence or comonotone assumptions (Perez-Diaz et al., 2025), or learning copula structures on top of marginal forecasts (Drouin et al., 2022; Ashok et al., 2024). On the other hand, diffusionor flow-matching-based generative time-series models are naturally well-suited for capturing joint trajectory distributions even without these ad hoc methods, as they can generate complete future paths while maintaining temporal and cross-variable dependencies. Unfortunately, existing generative models (Kollovieh et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) achieve neither high marginal accuracy nor efficient sampling, limiting their practical utility in real-world forecasting scenarios. This leads us to ask: Can we construct generative time-series model that achieves both high marginal accuracy and efficient sampling while also preserving trajectory dependence? We introduce PathFM to combine joint and multi-mode trajectory modeling with accurate marginal forecasting and efficient sampling. The model learns temporal and cross-variable dependence through conditional flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022), generating complete future paths conditioned on history and known future covariates. Parallel decoding distillation (Shaul et al., 2026) and history attention caching enable faster sampling with one or two model evaluations. To narrow the marginal accuracy gap, we add calibration loss that directly optimizes fair CRPS on generated forecasts. The distilled sampler makes this optimization practical by allowing calibration gradients to pass through its short rollout and refine the forecast distribution. With these components, PathFM-300M ranks second on the widely used fev-bench for marginal scores (Section 5).1 On Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which we curate to evaluate trajectory quality, PathFM ranks first for path scores (Section 5). In separate evaluation on chaotic systems, our sampling approach improves point forecast accuracy upon the state-of-the-art PANDA model, captures useful temporal dependence, and preserves long-run variability more faithfully than baselines 1Cutoff date for the rankings throughout this paper: Sept. 26, 2026; see Section A.1 for concurrent work.

sections.content: The velocity field uses transformer based on T5 (Raffel et al., 2020), with separate time and channel axes. Its inputs are patches of 16 values with masks and time indices, register token, and future patches populated by available covariates. Each block combines temporal self-attention, attention across channels at aligned patches, and pointwise feed-forward network. We condition flow time via adaptive RMS normalization (Chen et al., 2024) and apply QK normalization and weight decay. For reuse across paths, late entry separates conditioning from flow-dependent computation. The first blocks use unrestricted attention over history, the register, and future placeholders, without source noise or flow time. These representations incorporate the requested horizon and known future covariates. Restricting history attention before this stage would exclude that future information. Future positions then receive gated difference between flow-state and placeholder tokens. In subsequent blocks, history-only self-attention keeps history independent of the sampled path: history tokens attend only to history, while future tokens attend to both history and future. Flow-time modulation acts only on register and future tokens. Section B.1 specifies the configuration. Packing and caching. sections.title: 4 EVALUATING TRAJECTORY FORECASTS
sections.content: Trajectory forecasts should capture temporal dependence and accurately quantify uncertainty. Marginal accuracy alone cannot establish this. We introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench) to evaluate these properties alongside marginal scores. The benchmark combines established scoring rules into common protocol for constructing and comparing finite trajectory ensembles. Six complementary path scores. Different downstream queries depend on different aspects of path, motivating the complementary diagnostics in Table 7. Following the aggregation-andtransformation framework of Pic et al. (2025), we score both complete paths and transformations that expose these aspects. Energy score assesses the distribution of level paths, while differenced energy score emphasizes local changes by scoring the initial level and subsequent increments. Variogram score compares pairwise temporal contrasts to probe how values vary together across time (Scheuerer & Hamill, 2015). We then apply scalar CRPS to the horizon total, maximum, and first-passage time to assess accumulated uncertainty, extremes, and event timing. Specifically, first-passage time records the first crossing of history-derived threshold. fps-bench evaluates 94 fev-bench tasks (Shchur et al., 2025), excluding those with NaN values that prevent computing some path scores. Quantile-model completions. Applying these scores requires complete paths, which marginal quantile forecasts do not specify. We retain native samples when available. To include quantile models, we construct paths from their marginal quantiles under two explicit dependence assumptions. Sorted quantiles define piecewise-linear inverse CDF with constant extension beyond the outer quantiles. An independent completion draws separate quantile rank at each forecast time and channel, whereas comonotone completion shares one rank across an items times and channels. Both laws preserve the same underlying interpolated marginals, allowing us to examine how the dependence assumption affects trajectory scores. These two choices serve as baselines, as different dependence assumptions may yield different scores for the same marginal forecasts. Section D.1 specifies the score definitions, estimators, and aggregation.

sections.title: 5 FORECASTING ACCURACY AND EFFICIENCY
sections.content: We evaluate forecasts through their marginal accuracy, the path quality scores, and the cost of generating an ensemble. The experiments establish where trajectory forecasts help, then examine how distillation and score refinement make those forecasts practical. Section 6 complements these experiments with study of chaotic systems, with particular focus on long-run dynamics.

sections.title: 6 FORECASTING CHAOTIC DYNAMICS
sections.content: Chaotic systems pose sharp test of forecasting: can model preserve statistical structure after losing alignment with particular future? We compare fine-tuned Chronos-2, PANDA (Lai et al., 2026), and PathFM on point forecasting and long continuations of 135 DYSTS systems (Gilpin, 2021). We evaluate PathFM with ten-step Euler sampling per 256-step block. Section gives its training recipe, and evaluation details. 6.1 FORECAST ACCURACY AND DYNAMICAL FIDELITY Using sMAPE as in PANDA (Lai et al., 2026), we evaluate forecasts at horizons 64, 128, 256, and 512. sections.title: 7 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
sections.content: PathFM combines flow matching, distillation, shared computation, and direct score refinement to generate complete future trajectories efficiently. Its strongest gains concern the quality of complete trajectories and the downstream predictions they support. The dynamical study shows unique benefit: independently continued paths preserve variability that point forecasts can lose. Several limitations remain. PathFM does not yet support conditioning on modalities beyond time series, such as text. For chaotic systems, all four dynamical diagnostics remain well above the held-out-truth reference  (Table 2)  . Accurately recovering the invariant distribution remains an open challenge. key direction for future work is to continue scaling the backbone and training data, pushing the frontier of generative time series forecasting. sections.title: A RELATED WORK
sections.content: Marginal forecasting. Chronos-2, TimesFM-3, and Toto 2.0 provide direct marginal quantiles while sharing information across variables (Ansari et al., 2025; Jain & Sen, 2026; Khwaja et al., 2026). Toto 1.0 instead predicts marginal Student-t mixtures and samples forecasts autoregressively across output patches (Cohen et al., 2025). Perez-Diaz et al. (2025) distinguish forecast products by their operational uses and show that marginals do not identify path-dependent event probabilities. PathFM represents the joint forecast through complete multivariate paths, so the same samples support marginal summaries and distributions of trajectory-dependent quantities. Generative trajectory forecasting. DeepAR samples temporally dependent futures autoregressively (Salinas et al., 2020), and TACTiS learns multivariate predictive distributions with attentional copulas (Drouin et al., 2022). TimeGrad introduces autoregressive diffusion for multivariate forecasting (Rasul et al., 2021). Flow matching learns generative vector fields through conditional probability paths (Lipman et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2026); TSFlow incorporates Gaussian-process priors (Kollovieh et al., 2025), and Sundial uses flow matching for foundation-model pretraining (Liu et al., 2025). PathFM shares history computation across paths and uses distillation to support fast ensembles and direct forecast-score training. Distillation and direct score optimization. Flow map methods learn finite-time transport and support both teacher distillation and self-distillation (Boffi et al., 2024; 2026). Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) predicts multiple integration updates per network evaluation (Shaul et al., 2026). DRaFT optimizes differentiable rewards by backpropagating through diffusion sampling (Clark et al., 2024). Rewarded Moment Matching Distillation (RMMD) combines reward optimization with moment-matching supervision and applies unbiased sample CRPS to GenCast (Jacq et al., 2026). Its reward gradient passes through denoising step applied to re-noised student sample. PathFM backpropagates fair CRPS through the complete source-to-forecast map of one distilled evaluation. The same optimization updates continue matching the frozen teachers joint velocity field while fitting the students marginals to observations. Distillation thus supplies both short path for score gradients and continued supervision from joint generative teacher. Section 3.3 and table 4 give the objective and post-training comparisons. Forecast evaluation. Proper scoring rules underpin forecast comparison (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007). Fair scores address finite-ensemble effects (Ferro, 2014); variogram and transformation-based scores expose complementary multivariate properties (Scheuerer & Hamill, 2015; Pic et al., 2025). fps-bench combines these principles on fev-bench tasks (Shchur et al., 2025) to assess temporal dependence and trajectory-dependent quantities alongside marginal accuracy. DYSTS supplies interpretable chaotic systems (Gilpin, 2021), while PANDA studies pretraining across chaotic dynamics (Lai et al., 2026). Together, these evaluations test the value of complete forecast paths through downstream uncertainty, short-term tracking, and long-run dynamical fidelity. A.1 CONCURRENT WORK Time series foundation models are advancing rapidly. t0-gamma alternates temporal and variate attention to incorporate historical and known-future covariates (Meyer et al., 2026). It averages weights from five fine-tuned checkpoints into one 256M-parameter model (The Forecasting Company, 2026). QiYao-M fuses numerical patches with text and image embeddings (Cheng et al., 2026), but treats each target channel independently. EXAONE 1.0 specializes at financial forecasting and mixes time with causal convolutions and variates with groupwise pooling MLPs (Lee et al., 2026). All three models predict marginal quantiles, leaving dependence across future times and variables unspecified. PathFM retains its advantage in directly generating joint multivariate trajectories, combining learned temporal and cross-variable dependence with fast sampling and marginal calibration.

sections.content: Optimization and stage transitions. The recipe uses AdamW with (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.99) and global gradient-norm clipping at 1. Both models use weight decay 0.01 during flow matching and WSD. An optimizer update contains 1,024 channel rows. Terminal decay continues the flow model with its optimizer and EMA state. PDD initializes the student from the terminal teachers EMA weights, freezes that teacher, and starts fresh optimizer. Calibration resumes the PDD student, optimizer, and EMA. Data and task sampling. Training uses 83M-row dataset of real-world and synthetic time series, including both univariate and multivariate data. Training samples contexts up to 8,192 time steps and forecast horizons up to 480 time steps. During training, we randomly sample context and forecast lengths within these limits. Post-training objectives. PDD trains the backbone and twenty interval heads on uniform time grid, using the block-size menu {1, 2, 5, 10, 20}, on-policy states, Euler teacher labels, and tiled residual heads. Calibration retains path-wise PDD and adds fair CRPS with coefficient one on each loss, globally normalized over scored coordinates. The CRPS term uses eight iid paths, one parallel evaluation, and the same Gaussian source scale as flow training and inference. Main benchmark results use the final EMA checkpoint after all four stages. The architecture, distillation, and refinement controls below retain their stated training budgets. B.3 DISTILLATION AND EVALUATION BUDGET Figure 8 reports teacherstudent inference budget comparison in both model sizes. Each pair is evaluated at 1, 2, 4, and 10 sequential network evaluations (NFE). Figure 8: Teacherstudent accuracy at different evaluation budgets. Rows show teacherstudent pairs from the 126M and 295M families; columns show FEV and six-component FPS skill, with higher values preferred. NFE uses logarithmic horizontal axis. Thin vertical bars show pointwise 95% task-bootstrap intervals from 2,000 resamples. At one evaluation, PDD avoids the teachers sharp loss of accuracy and has higher skill scores than the ten-evaluation teacher in both pairs. Additional evaluations give no consistent improvement. These results show that the student preserves the teachers forecasting accuracy at much lower budget.

sections.title: F CHAOTIC SYSTEMS
sections.content: We examine how model size, sampling, and fine-tuning affect point accuracy and long-run dynamics. F.1 SETUP AND FORECASTING PROTOCOLS Dataset. We train PathFM on the PANDA-72M reproduction corpus (Lai et al., 2026), GilpinLab/dataset-panda72M-repro, containing 190,006 trajectories of 4,096 steps with 310 state coordinates from individual DYSTS systems and skew-product combinations. Reserving trajectories involving ten parent systems leaves 156,784 training trajectories and 33,222 validation trajectories. Point evaluation uses the separate base40 and skew40 test releases. Models and training. The quantitative comparisons use the 75M and 126M PathFM families with native 256-step horizons, trained for 2M flow-matching updates followed by 100k terminal-decay updates. We train the 75M variant to approximately match PANDAs parameter count (74.2M versus 71.6M). The 126M backbone has 12 transformer blocks and feedforward width 3,072; the 75M model uses 11 blocks and width 768. Both initialize their backbones afresh while retaining trainable input-patch embeddings. The global batch budget is 384 channel rows, with four flow draws per window. The learning rate is 104 after 500 warmup updates, followed by the 100k linear terminal decay to zero; weight decay is zero and EMA decay is 0.999. Main results use ten-step Euler sampling, source standard deviation 0.86, and seed 42. Training-progress evaluation. Figure 6c uses the same 2,048 fixed three-channel validation windows for both model sizes, selected randomly from the validation shard. Each window supplies 512 context steps and 256 forecast steps from distinct held-out trajectory. We evaluate EMA weights with 16 stratified samples and ten Euler steps. Context-standardized sMAPE is averaged over channels and forecast steps, then across the 2,048 trajectories. Point forecasts. We evaluate six 512-context windows from each of 9,347 trajectories using sMAPE, as in PANDA (Lai et al., 2026). We average sMAPE within each of the 480 source groups and then report the arithmetic mean across groups. PathFM feeds back the coordinatewise median of 16 stratified samples per 256-step block, averaging the middle two order statistics. Chronos-1 uses
